en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Section on the Refutation of Difficulties (Meṇḍakapañha Paṇāmitavagga)
1. The Question on the Best Dhamma “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘For the Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, is the best among people, both in this present life and in the life to come.’”

Furthermore, it is said: “A lay follower who is a stream-enterer—one for whom the states of woe are closed, who has attained right view and understood the teaching—bows down to or rises up before a monk or a novice who is still an ordinary person.
If, venerable Nāgasena, the Blessed One has said:
“For the Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, is the best among people in this visible world and in the life to come,” then by that...

Indeed, as for the statement: "A lay follower, a householder, a stream-enterer who has closed off the states of woe, attained to right view, and understood the teaching, bows down to and rises up before a monk or a novice who is still an ordinary person"—that is false. If [one were to say]:
"A lay follower, a householder, a stream-enterer who has closed off the states of woe, attained to right view, and understood the teaching..."

“Or [if one thinks]: ‘I salute and rise up for a worldling’—then, Vāseṭṭha, that statement of yours, ‘The Dhamma is indeed the best among people, both in this present life and in the life to come,’ would also be false.
This too is a double-pronged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.”
“Great King, this was indeed said by the Blessed One: ‘For the Dhamma, Vāseṭṭha, is the best among people, both in this present life and in the life to come.

And it was said: ‘A lay follower who is a stream-enterer, for whom the states of deprivation are closed off, who has attained right view and understood the teaching, should pay homage to and rise up before a bhikkhu or a novice, even if that person is an ordinary worldling.’”
In this matter, however, there is a reason. What is that reason?
Great King, there are these twenty qualities that make one an ascetic, and two outward signs, by which an ascetic becomes worthy of salutation, rising from one's seat, honoring, and worship.
What are the twenty qualities that make a recluse a recluse, and the two characteristics?

They are: delighting in the supreme Dhamma, the foremost restraint, conduct, dwelling, self-restraint, control, patience, gentleness, solitary wandering, delight in solitude, seclusion, moral shame, moral dread, energy, heedfulness, undertaking the training, recitation, and interrogation.

Delight in virtue and so forth, homelessness, fulfillment of the training rules, wearing the saffron robe, and being a mendicant—these, O Great King, are the twenty qualities that make one a recluse, along with the two outward signs.
A bhikkhu conducts himself by undertaking these qualities; because they are not deficient, because they are complete, and because they are perfected, [he is a true recluse].
Because he is endowed with these qualities, he enters the stage of one beyond training (*asekkhabhūmi*), the stage of an arahant; he enters the most excellent state among states.
Since he has drawn near to arahantship, it is fitting for a stream-enterer lay follower to bow down to and rise up before a bhikkhu who is still an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).

"He has attained the same spiritual status as those whose taints are destroyed; there is no [other] occasion for me [to do otherwise]," thus it is fitting for a stream-enterer lay follower to bow down to and rise up before a bhikkhu who is still an ordinary person.

‘He has entered the foremost assembly, whereas I have not entered that assembly’—for this reason, a lay follower who is a stream-enterer ought to pay homage to and rise for a bhikkhu who is an ordinary person.

‘He is able to hear the recitation of the Pātimokkha, whereas I am not able to hear it’—for this reason, a lay follower who is a stream-enterer ought to pay homage to and rise for a bhikkhu who is an ordinary person.

‘He ordains others and grants full admission, thereby increasing the teaching of the Conqueror, whereas I am not able to do this’—for this reason, a lay follower who is a stream-enterer ought to pay homage to and rise for a bhikkhu who is still an ordinary person.

‘He practices fully those training rules that are immeasurable, whereas I do not conduct myself according to them’—for this reason, a lay follower who is a stream-enterer ought to pay homage to and rise for a bhikkhu who is still an ordinary person.

‘He has entered upon the mark of a recluse and stands in the intention of a Buddha; therefore, because of that mark, I am far removed [from such a state]. Thus a stream-entering lay follower ought to pay homage to and rise for a bhikkhu who is still an ordinary person.

‘His hair and body hair are grown long, he is neither anointed nor adorned, but is anointed with the fragrance of virtue; whereas I delight in adornment and decoration. Thus a stream-entering lay follower ought to pay homage to and rise for a bhikkhu who is still an ordinary person.
Moreover, Great King, regarding those twenty qualities that constitute a recluse and the two outward signs—
since all these qualities are found in a bhikkhu, and he alone maintains them and trains others therein,
whereas I have neither such attainment nor the ability to train others— a lay follower who is a stream-enterer ought to pay homage to and rise for a bhikkhu who is still an ordinary person.

“Just as, great king, a prince studies the sciences in the presence of a family priest and trains in the duties of a kshatriya, and at a later time, having been consecrated, he pays homage to his teacher and rises for him, thinking, ‘This man is my instructor’;

even so, great king, because ‘the bhikkhu is an instructor and a bearer of the lineage,’ it is fitting for a lay follower who is a stream-enterer to pay homage to and rise for a bhikkhu who is still an ordinary person.
Moreover, great king, by this method you should understand the greatness and the incomparable vastness of the bhikkhu’s state.”

“If, Great King, a lay follower who is a stream-enterer realizes Arhatship, he has only two destinations and no other: on that very day he would either attain Parinibbāna or enter the state of a monk.
For that going forth, Great King, is immovable, vast, and exalted—namely, the stage of a monk.

“It is a matter of knowledge, venerable Nāgasena; this question has been well unraveled by you, who are powerful and of exceeding intelligence. No one else is capable of unraveling this question in such a way, except for an intelligent person like yourself.”
The first question on the supreme Dhamma.
